verdicts.REASON: Source names the Edinburgh art festival and states the mode: 'You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.'
Verbatim: 'By the time you’re done with Edinburgh art festival you’ll have uncovered so many hidden stories you’ll feel like Columbo.'
Source is a first-person review ('don’t do a lot for me', 'I love it'), so attributing the formulation to the reviewer is directly licensed.
'But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing.'
'There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects'.
'and it’s impossible to figure out how any of it fits together' — stated by the reviewer, and attributed as such.
Metaphorical restatement ('no map that resolves it') of the source-given 'impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'. Adds no world-state content.
'You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.'
Synthesis of two grounded facts — 'the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded' plus the gallery-after-gallery unknown-name claim. No new content about the world.
'You can’t walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you’ve never heard of.'
Draws out the shape of the source's own claim about unknown names in every gallery; 'without preparation' is the article's reading, not a new fact.
A statement about the article's own selection procedure, disclaiming a ranking the source never makes. No world-state content added.
'Sandra George (1957-2013)'.
'She was a black photographer and photojournalist who documented life on the margins of inner city Edinburgh.'
'She captured protests and action groups operating out of living rooms and town halls'.
'people living in hostels and housing schemes'.
'There are kids everywhere, always playing and laughing, often in desperately bleak places.'
'She appears throughout her show at City Art Gallery in self-portraits, often with her young son.'
'Like a lot of people in EAF, she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime' — the typicality is the source's own framing.
'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
'and was only discovered after her death in 2013'.
'Frank Walter (1926-2009)'.
'an Antiguan painter, writer, poet and polymath'.
'The group show at Ingleby Gallery is good, too. It’s all centred on Frank Walter'.
'who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'.
'His work is small, subtle, strange.'
'He paints on ripped cardboard and fading paper'.
'he depicts rainbows and stars and smiling faces'.
'strange trees that bend and twist at weird angles'.

A positional claim about the source. The duty passage sits in the last third of the review (13th of 19 paragraphs), not at its midpoint, but 'midway' is a loose narrative connective with no fixed threshold. Resolved by whether the article means structural midpoint or rough middle stretch.
Characterising 'I think they have a duty' as a demand is the article naming the shape of a quoted statement; no world-state content added.
'If contemporary artists and institutions want to tell hidden stories' — the conditional is the source's own.
'I think they have a duty – to viewers and to their subjects – to tell them clearly', correctly attributed to the reviewer.
'a duty – to viewers and to their subjects' names exactly two addressees.
Evaluative comparison of the two addressees the source itself supplies. It is the article's reading of a grounded pair, not a fact about the world, a person, or the source's position.
The article's gloss on what clarity toward viewers consists of, reasoning about the source-given duty. Adds no world-state content.
'The handout talks about vibrations, energy, AI, weather systems in Texas. It’s mind-meltingly indecipherable.'
'is let down by some wispy, barely contextualised lumps and scrawls'.
Transitional sentence marking the article's own move between the two addressees; asserts nothing about the world.
The article reasoning about the duty-to-subjects the source states; a reading, not a new fact.
Instruction to the reader structuring the article's own argument; no world-state content.
Recurrence is checkable in the source: 'undiscovered archives', 'only discovered after her death', 'Another largely undiscovered artist', 'previously undiscovered marginalised artist'.
'We’re talking queer narratives, secret histories, undiscovered archives'.
'Another largely undiscovered artist, Sadao Hasegawa (1945-1999)'.
'hope you sniff out something you like'.
'“You’ve never heard of this previously undiscovered marginalised artist? You bastard!”' — the source stages exactly this scolding.
The article's assessment of the weight the word carries, based on recurrences it has already grounded.
Reading of the source's visit-scale usage ('by the time you’re done', 'follow your nose'); 'afternoon' is figurative shorthand for the visit, not an asserted duration.
'her show at City Art Gallery' — a festival venue named by the source.
'The group show at Ingleby Gallery is good, too.'
'an eye-popping display of throbbing members and gushing penetration at Custom Lane'.
The article's reading of how the source uses 'discovery' — located in the viewer's present. No new content about the world.
The source presents nose-following as the only available route ('You’ve just got to…') and the reviewer evidently toured the festival; the inference is directly licensed.
Extends the source's 'EAF is too big and complex… to really make sense' to the city-wide field the source itself describes ('a city-wide art festival'). Figurative transfer, not a new factual claim.
Transitional instruction organising the article's own argument.
'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime'.
'and was only discovered after her death in 2013'.
'who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime'.
'Another largely undiscovered artist, Sadao Hasegawa (1945-1999)… at Custom Lane'.

The source qualifies: 'Most of the Japanese illustrator’s work… stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.' The proposition drops 'most' and asserts it of all his work — an absolute produced by removing the source's qualifier.
The article's analysis of whose experience the source's 'discovery' vocabulary tracks; built on quoted usages, adds nothing about the world.
Definitional gloss on the source's own usage; no world-state content.
The article's argument about what the source's vocabulary leaves unnamed, resting on the life-dates and unshown-in-lifetime facts the source supplies.

Source states it outright for George ('she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime') and Walter ('died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings'), the artists whose dates the passage is measuring.
